subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Dark Matter: The Invisible Glue
description: A quick, practical guide to Dark Matter: The Invisible Glue.

hook.text: 85% of all matter in the universe is invisible. It doesn't emit or absorb light. We call it dark matter.

buildup.text: Fritz Zwicky noticed in 1933 that galaxies in clusters moved too fast. Visible mass couldn't explain their speed.

discovery.text: Vera Rubin confirmed it in the 1970s. Galaxy edges rotate as fast as their centers—impossible without extra hidden mass.

twist.text: We don't know what dark matter is. It's not black holes, not gas, not stars. It may be an undiscovered particle.

climax.text: Underground detectors and particle colliders are hunting for dark matter particles. So far, nothing has been found.

punchline.text: Eighty-five percent of all matter. Totally invisible. Still unknown.

quiz.question: How did scientists first detect evidence for dark matter?
options: Galaxies and clusters moved faster than visible matter alone could explain
Dark matter particles were captured in underground detectors
Telescopes observed dark regions blocking background starlight

details.summary: Dark matter is an invisible substance that makes up about 27% of the universe's total energy content. It doesn't emit, absorb, or reflect light, but its gravitational effects are unmistakable — galaxies rotate too fast, galaxy clusters are too massive, and the CMB pattern requires it.
details.whyItMatters: Dark matter holds galaxies together and shaped the universe's large-scale structure. Without it, galaxies would fly apart and the cosmic web would never have formed. Identifying dark matter is one of physics' greatest unsolved problems.
takeaways: Dark matter comprises about 27% of the universe's energy content
It's invisible but detected through its gravitational effects
Its identity remains one of physics' greatest mysteries

faq.question: What are the leading dark matter candidates?
faq.answer: WIMPs (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) were long favored but haven't been detected despite extensive searches. Axions — extremely light particles proposed to solve a separate physics puzzle — are gaining attention. Primordial black holes and sterile neutrinos are other possibilities.

faq.question: Could dark matter just be normal matter we can't see?
faq.answer: No. Big Bang nucleosynthesis precisely predicts the amount of normal matter from observed light element ratios. Only about 5% of the universe is normal matter. The extra gravitational mass must be something fundamentally different — a new type of particle or substance unknown to current physics.
